key_insight: When many distinct experimental environments are available but observations are unpaired (we see X or Y, not both), treating the environment as a high-dimensional instrument and leveraging sparsity lets you identify and estimate causal effects despite hidden confounding.
problem_solved: How to recover causal effect estimates under hidden confounding from fragmented/unpaired experimental data with many experiments but few or no repeated joint X–Y observations per environment.
method: Recast the unpaired-data problem as an instrumental variable regression where the environment label serves as (possibly high-dimensional) instrument.
Exploit sparsity in the causal effect vector and aggregate cross-environment moment information to achieve identification when individual experiments have few repetitions.

Use regularized estimation / dimension-reduction across environments (e.g., sparse estimation and moment-based IV techniques) to recover stable causal effect estimates despite unpaired samples and hidden confounding.
impact: Enables practitioners to obtain credible causal estimates from fragmented experimental datasets common in large-scale systems and hardware/infra settings, reducing the need for costly paired experiments and informing robust interventions.
visual_elements: Schematic: many environments → some provide X, others provide Y; environment label points to both X and Y (instrumental role).
Diagram: sparse effect vector (few nonzero coefficients) highlighted among many covariates.
Chart: heatmap or bar chart showing many environments on x-axis, low sample counts per environment, and aggregated moments used for estimation.
Flowchart: data (unpaired) → form instrument from environments → sparse IV estimation → causal effect output.
paper_title: Many Experiments, Few Repetitions, Unpaired Data, and Sparse Effects: Is Causal Inference Possible?
paper_authors: Felix Schur, Niklas Pfister, Peng Ding, Sach Mukherjee, Jonas Peters
